source: Hu, Long, Wang (2026) When Continual Learning Moves to Memory: A Study of Experience Reuse in LLM Agents
finding: Frozen-weights agents with external memory still show continual-learning interference. It moves from weights to retrieval: old and new experiences compete for a limited context window. Abstract insights transfer and forget less than raw trajectories. Negative transfer hits the hard cases most.
numbers: ALFWorld and BabyAI, ReAct agent with ReMe memory, 200 training instances per phase (Task A then Task B), 100 test instances. BabyAI backward transfer (B then A): Insight memory +3.5 points, Raw memory -4.0. Fine-grained per-step memory (Cond-Ind) gave +15.0% forward transfer but BWT -10.0%; the compact variant (Cond-Agg) forgot less.
quote: relocating the continual-learning bottleneck from parameter updates to memory access
limits: Preprint. Two benchmark families, one memory module. No replay or regression-set step was tested. Disagrees with Zhang 2026 on whether abstraction is the safer store.
agent_relevance: Our lesson store will have its own forgetting. Measure backward transfer (old-task accuracy after new lessons) per lesson batch. Keep the store compact.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Useful Memories Become Faulty When Continuously Updated by LLMs
finding: When an LLM rewrites past trajectories into a lesson bank, utility first rises and then falls, and can drop below no memory. Even with ground-truth solutions fed in, the consolidated memory broke problems the model had solved. An episodic-only control (raw trajectories, no abstraction) stayed competitive. Letting the agent choose Retain/Delete/Consolidate doubled accuracy over forced consolidation.
numbers: ARC-AGI Stream, GPT-5.4: a 19-problem slice solved 100% without memory fell to 54% with consolidation. Ten runs on 33 tasks solvable without memory: mean accuracy 58.5 (no memory), 55.1 (epoch 1), 38.5 (epoch 10); tasks still solved at pass@10: 100%, 66.7% (22/33), 60.6% (20/33).
quote: robust agent memory should treat raw episodes as first-class evidence and gate consolidation explicitly rather than firing it after every interaction
limits: Preprint v2 (Aug 2026). ARC-style tasks dominate; WebShop, ALFWorld and AppWorld show episodic-only is competitive. Regression is measured against a no-memory solved set, not a replayed regression set. It does not test replay of old problems before commit.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct evidence that regression at lesson-write time is real and large. Re-test the old solved set after every consolidation. Keep raw episodes as evidence; treat distilled rules as rewritable views.

source: Tablan, Taylor, Bernhem (2026) Learning on the Job: Continual Learning from Deployment Feedback for Frozen-Weights Agents
finding: A frozen model plus a store of natural-language rules distilled from each episode improves a lot on tau-bench banking. The paper reports a hold rate (a task passed at trial t passes again at t+1) as the retention measure. Distilled instruction rules held banked solutions less well than stored experience. The writer prompt forbids contradicting a VERIFIED RULE.
numbers: tau-bench banking, 97 tasks, 4 trials. Mistral Large pass^1: no memory 0.103, experience 0.170 (32/97 solved). Learning from outcome verdicts gave 1.6x and from corrections 2.6x the static-RAG baseline; 22 of 84 never-solved tasks converted. Hold rate: experience 0.88, instruction 0.65, paired contrast -0.23 [-0.47, -0.02]. Claude Sonnet 5 replication: no memory pass^1 0.248 (40/97), instruction 0.397 (62/97), hold 0.83.
limits: Preprint, one benchmark domain, memory-vendor authors. Hold rate measures repeat success, not damage of a new lesson to old unrelated tasks. No replay arm.
agent_relevance: Gives a cheap metric (hold rate or regression rate) for our regression set. Distilled rules lost 0.23 hold vs raw experience, which agrees with Zhang 2026. Locking verified rules is a crude schema-consistency gate.

source: Wu, Ding, Huang, Zhao (2026) Forget to Improve: On-Device LLM-Agent Continual Learning via Budget-Curated Memory (CURATOR)
finding: Scores each memory entry as value minus harm per byte and evicts low scorers. Pruning by net value cut memory and removed poisoned or stale entries without losing accuracy. Replay-by-success alone can keep over-specific or adversarial entries.
numbers: Abstract: memory reduced 2.7x, uplink 2.4x, injection success 0.75 to zero, on task-drift benchmarks and a Jetson testbed. A recency-only baseline sat near accuracy 0.33 with injection success 0.75 (text, one setting).
limits: Preprint, edge-device setting aimed at poisoning and budget, not interference between lessons. Value and harm scores are the method's own.
agent_relevance: Supports pruning lessons by measured harm. It is a salience-style score for what to keep, not a test of salience-weighted replay for regression.

source: Zheng et al. (2025) Spurious Forgetting in Continual Learning of Language Models (ICLR 2025)
finding: Accuracy on an old task collapses within about 150 steps of new-task fine-tuning, yet the knowledge is still there. Fine-tuning on half of the old data (not overlapping the test half) restores it almost fully. Training on ten irrelevant or safety instances also restores it. The loss is task alignment, not knowledge.
numbers: Task 0 accuracy fell from near 100% to about 10% in 150 steps (20% at the end). Recovered accuracy stayed near 100% through the first 150 steps and was 96% at the end of Task 1. Freeze (bottom layers fixed) raised sequential fine-tuning accuracy from 11% to 44%; other methods peaked at 22%.
quote: performance on older tasks could be restored by training on merely ten safety instances or irrelevant tasks
limits: The recovery step is a weight update on old-task data, not a prompt re-cue. Mostly a synthetic setup plus some real continual-instruction tests. Replay of 20% old data did not remove the alignment drop.
agent_relevance: Forgetting may be a cueing problem, so an agent can try a cheap re-cue before declaring a regression. But the shown recovery trains on old items; for us that means showing old examples in context. Untested in prompts.

source: Zheng et al. (2025) Spurious Forgetting (LAMOL generative replay analysis)
finding: Self-generated pseudo old samples are poor. After filtering for format, duplicates and exact match to real old data, fewer than 20% of 24,000 pseudo samples survive, so nearly half are hallucinated. Real stored old data does much better.
numbers: LAMOL generated 24,000 pseudo old samples (20% of the new data). Fewer than 20% remained valid after filtering.
limits: Same paper as d05, so not an independent source. Compares generation quality, not an agent prompt store. Results-table cell mapping was too garbled to quote.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 3 for weights: once the generator is an LLM, real replay beats model-generated replay. For us, store the real old problem and its verified answer; do not ask the model to imagine regression tests.

source: Kotha, Springer, Raghunathan (2024) Understanding Catastrophic Forgetting in Language Models via Implicit Inference (ICLR 2024)
finding: Fine-tuning improves in-distribution tasks while the model implicitly infers which task a prompt is and is skewed toward the fine-tuned tasks. Changing the prompt so the task looks far from the fine-tuning data (Conjugate Prompting, for example translation) recovers lost abilities with no weight update.
numbers: Alpaca ICL input drop: Leetspeak 1.0%, French 29.00%, English 56.75%. For an instruction-tuned model, answer frequency in English fell from 92% to 3%, but in Malayalam only 71% to 65%.
limits: Synthetic linear-function setup plus a few real tests. Mechanism (task inference) differs from Zheng's (alignment loss). Recovery is partial.
agent_relevance: Supports a verify-by-recueing step: re-pose the old problem in a different surface form before concluding it regressed. This is prompt-level, so usable. It does not remove the need for a regression set.

source: Lin, Snell, Wang, Packer et al. (2025) Sleep-time Compute: Beyond Inference Scaling at Test-time
finding: Pre-computing inferences about a stored context before the query arrives cuts test-time tokens at equal accuracy. Gains are larger when the query is predictable from the context.
numbers: Stateful GSM-Symbolic and Stateful AIME: about 5x less test-time compute at equal accuracy; scaling sleep-time compute adds up to +13% (GSM) and +18% (AIME). Multi-Query GSM-Symbolic: average cost per query down 2.5x.
quote: predictability of the user query to be well correlated with the efficacy of sleep-time compute
limits: Single paper. Benchmarks were rebuilt so context and query are separable. Pareto-dominates pass@k at equal test-time tokens on these tasks.
agent_relevance: An offline pass pays when later queries are predictable from stored lessons. Candidate for an idle-time re-verification pass over the lesson store.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Sleep-time Compute, Sec. 6 SWE-Features case study
finding: On a realistic agentic coding task, offline compute helped only at low test-time budgets. At high test-time budgets plain test-time compute was better, with higher precision.
numbers: Up to about 1.5x fewer test-time tokens at low budgets on SWE-Features. At high budget, test-time-only had higher precision and similar recall; the sleep-time agent edited more files.
quote: when the test-time compute budget is high, using only test-time compute can perform better
limits: Same paper as d08. Benchmark built by the authors. Sleep-time token cost is not netted against savings except in the multi-query result.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 5 partly: the 5x figure shrinks to about 1.5x on a real agent task and reverses at high budget. An offline consolidation pass needs a break-even test on our own tasks.

source: Lampinen, Chan, Pascanu, Shanahan, McClelland et al. (2025) On the generalization of language models from in-context learning and finetuning: a controlled study
finding: With the same data, in-context learning generalizes to reversals and syllogisms better than fine-tuning. Fine-tuning on in-context reasoning traces (offline learning by thinking) closes much of the gap. Some reversal failures vanish when the fact sits inside a larger structure of knowledge.
numbers: Reversal-curse data: fine-tuning near floor, in-context near ceiling (from Fig. 2 text). On nonsense reversals the in-context benefit is weaker. The 12% and 6% oracle-retrieval figures were not found in this paper; they belong to the latent-learning paper (c02).
quote: in-context learning over the entire training dataset often generalizes better than finetuning
limits: Pretrained models, controlled synthetic facts. Whole dataset in context, so not a retrieval test.
agent_relevance: For a frozen agent the store is in context, the stronger learner here. The offline step that pays is generating implied inferences (reversals, derived facts) and storing them, which matches sleep-time compute. Gap 8's practice question for retrieval stays open.

source: Soutif-Cormerais et al. (2023) A Comprehensive Empirical Evaluation on Online Continual Learning (ICCV workshop)
finding: An independent group reran many replay methods under one tuned protocol. No method wins on all metrics or memory sizes. Well-tuned plain ER is very competitive. Most methods under-fit.
numbers: Split-CIFAR100 (20 tasks), memory 2000, 5 seeds, final accuracy: MIR 30.4 +-0.8, DER++ 29.9 +-0.6, ER-ACE 29.4 +-1.9. Split-TinyImagenet, memory 4000: MIR 22.7 +-1.1, DER++ 23.6 +-0.7, ER-ACE 21.3 +-0.8.
quote: Well properly tuned ER is a very competitive baseline
limits: Image classification only. CLS-ER, FearNet and DualNet were not in the comparison, so dual-memory claims remain untested here. Other table rows were garbled.
agent_relevance: Fancy replay variants add little over a tuned simple buffer. Start with plain stored exemplars; prioritisation must beat it to be worth building.

source: Buzzega, Boschini, Porrello, Calderara (2020) Rethinking Experience Replay: a Bag of Tricks for Continual Learning
finding: Naive rehearsal with five small fixes matches or beats sophisticated rehearsal methods. Tuning and implementation details explain much of the published gaps.
numbers: Accuracy gains of 51.2 points (CIFAR-10) and 26.9 points (CIFAR-100) over plain ER at buffer size 1000.
quote: naive rehearsal can be patched to achieve similar performance
limits: Image tasks; same lab that made DER. Shows baselines are often under-tuned, but it is not an independent test of CLS-ER.
agent_relevance: Before crediting a dual-memory design, tune the single-store baseline at equal tokens.

source: Aljundi et al. (2019) Online Continual Learning with Maximally Interfered Retrieval (MIR)
finding: Replaying the stored items whose predictions the coming update would hurt most beats random replay, with modest accuracy gains and less forgetting.
numbers: MNIST Split: MIR beats the baseline by 2.8% accuracy and 2.5% forgetting. MinImagenet (100 memories per class, 3 updates): ER 24.7 acc and 23.5 forgetting vs ER-MIR 25.2 and 18.0. 15 to 20 runs per cell.
limits: Table cells partly garbled; text numbers used. Needs a gradient look-ahead that a prompt agent lacks. Accuracy gain small; forgetting gain larger.
agent_relevance: Prompt-level analogue: choose regression items most likely to conflict with the new lesson. Expect modest gains; test against random picks.

source: Schaul, Quan, Antonoglou, Silver (2016) Prioritized Experience Replay
finding: Replaying transitions with large prediction error more often speeds RL learning. A synthetic task shows exponential speed-ups with an oracle order.
numbers: DQN with prioritized replay beat DQN with uniform replay on 41 of 49 Atari games.
quote: outperforming DQN with uniform replay on 41 out of 49 games
limits: Reinforcement learning with TD error, not forgetting of old tasks. Needs bias correction. Not the same as Kumaran 2016's rare-and-salient claim.
agent_relevance: Supports prioritising by surprise or error when budget is small. Not a test of agent lesson regression.

source: Anagnostaras, Maren, Fanselow (1999) Temporally graded retrograde amnesia of contextual fear after hippocampal damage in rats: within-subjects examination
finding: Hippocampal lesions hurt contextual fear learned 1 day before surgery but spared fear learned 50 days before, in the same animals. Tone fear was spared in both. Sham animals' fear of the two contexts differed by about 1%.
numbers: Exp 1: 29 rats (DH 14, sham 15; final DH n=11); lesion x time F(1,24)=16, p<0.001. Peak context freezing, remote: sham 95.8+-2.0, DH 96.6+-2.4; recent: sham 95.8+-1.6, DH 71.6+-8.4. Exp 2: 28 rats, lesion 1 day after one training session, DH context 79.7+-9.1 vs sham 99.3+-0.7. Exp 3: 27 rats.
limits: Read through a fetch summary of the full text; table layout partly ambiguous. Only two delays (1 and 50 days): shows a gradient exists but cannot fit a decay rate. Electrolytic lesions in female rats.
agent_relevance: The graded-decay premise is real but coarse. Only 'recent hurts, old spared' is established here, not a rate per day.

source: Squire, Genzel, Wixted, Morris (2015) Memory consolidation (Cold Spring Harbor Perspectives in Biology)
finding: Graded retrograde amnesia is seen in monkeys, rats and mice, with gradients from days to months. Several labs report flat gradients (no sparing of old memories) in context fear and the water maze. Multiple-trace and transformation theory predict the hippocampus stays involved for detailed memories; the evidence is mixed.
numbers: Context fear: lesions 28 days after training spared freezing, 1 day did not (Kim and Fanselow 1992); 50-day sparing (Anagnostaras 1999); mouse inactivation impaired at 1 day, not 28 days (Wiltgen 2010). Tse 2007: pair learning took about 6 weeks, but lesions 3 hours after training impaired and 2 days after did not. Flat gradients: Lehmann 2007, Sutherland 2008, Sparks 2011, Broadbent and Clark 2013; water maze: Sutherland 2001, Clark 2005, 2007. Hippocampal patients rated 87.1% of childhood memories as remembered vs 80.3% for controls (Bayley 2005).
limits: Review favouring standard consolidation; read via a fetch summary of the first 100,000 characters. Group sizes absent. It says the gradient is seen too often to discount but it is unclear why it is not always seen.
agent_relevance: The 1995 time course is not fixed. Schema and memory type change the speed (Tse). Do not copy a decay constant; make the consolidation delay depend on schema fit.

source: Wiltgen, Sanders, Anagnostaras, Sage, Fanselow (2006) Context fear learning in the absence of the hippocampus (J Neurosci)
finding: Rats with hippocampal lesions before training learn context fear, though less well after one shock. With more trials they match controls, so a slower cortical route can learn the context. Lesions after 10 trials still gave severe retrograde amnesia at 14 days.
numbers: Exp 1: five shock delays, sham n=18, 17, 26, 20, 17 and lesion n=18, 18, 26, 18, 17; overall lesion effect F(1,185)=16.15, p<0.05. Exp 2: single-shock deficit F(1,72)=10.51; three shocks no deficit (F<1). Exp 3: sham 23, lesion 11; retrograde deficit F(1,32)=37.2; retraining with five trials no deficit.
limits: Freezing percentages only in figures. Read via fetch summary. Tests anterograde learning and a single 1-day lesion timepoint, not a graded curve.
agent_relevance: Matches CLS: a slow system can learn alone but needs more repetition. Single-trial lessons need the fast store; repeated lessons can be learned in slow form.

source: Gap-search negative result: agent-level interleaved replay at lesson-write time
finding: No paper found in this search interleaves old solved problems into the lesson-write step of a frozen-weights agent and measures regression at equal tokens. The closest are d01, d02 and d03, which measure regression without a replay arm.
numbers: Tools: one WebSearch returned 10 hits, then quota-blocked; arXiv API, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex rate-limited; one arXiv search page gave unreliable results. Not exhaustive.
limits: Absence of evidence under a limited search. Recent preprints may exist.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 2, 4 and 10 stay open and are good first experiments for our own harness.
